title: The Formalism Vault
topics: Hilbert space, hermitian operators, Dirac notation
spectral decomposition, projectors and the measurement postulate
Schrodinger and Heisenberg picture, Ehrenfest, conservation laws

sources.where: Question 2 [Heisenberg uncertainty relation, 18 pt], Question 3 [Heisenberg picture, 22 pt]
Part A, A2, A3, A4, A7 (adapted) and B.1 [QM in finite dimensions, 20 pt]

intro: The vault is where the rules of quantum mechanics are kept: states are vectors in a Hilbert space, observables are hermitian operators, a measurement projects onto an eigenspace, and noncommuting observables obey $\Delta A\Delta B\ge\frac12|\langle[A,B]\rangle|$. Exams ask the same set of proofs again and again (HS18 Q2 and Q3, FS22 Q3, HS22 A and B.1), so the derivation desk matters as much as the fights.

tutorial.title: The phase-space plate
tutorial.html: The horizontal axis is the width $\Delta x$ of a state, the vertical axis its momentum width $\Delta p$ (units $\hbar=1$). The glowing hyperbola is $\Delta x\Delta p=\hbar/2$: no state lives below it. The marker slides along it for Gaussian states; squeezing $\Delta x$ blows up $\Delta p$.

tutorial.title: The rotating dial
tutorial.html: The second marker is the Heisenberg-picture oscillator: $x_H(t)=x\cos\omega t+\frac{p}{m\omega}\sin\omega t$ rotates in phase space while the commutator $[x_H,p_H]=i\hbar$ is preserved (the area of the ellipse never shrinks).

tutorial.title: Consoles
tutorial.html: Library: four lessons (Hilbert space, projectors and measurement, uncertainty, time evolution). Quiz includes adapted HS22 part A items. Derivation desk: the proofs asked in HS18 Q2/Q3 and HS22 B.1. Fights: spin-1 measurement, Heisenberg picture of the oscillator, the stronger uncertainty relation. Boss gate: HS18 Q2, HS18 Q3, HS22 B.1.

encounters.title: Hilbert space, operators and Dirac notation

source.where: Ch. 4.1-4.4 (pp. 41-46): Hilbertraum, L2, Operatoren und Observable

blocks.html: A Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is a complex vector space with a positive-definite sesquilinear inner product $\langle\cdot|\cdot\rangle$ (script 4.2-4.4: linear in the second argument, $\langle\psi|\chi\rangle=\overline{\langle\chi|\psi\rangle}$, $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle\ge0$ with equality only for $\psi=0$) such that the induced norm $\|\psi\|=\sqrt{\langle\psi|\psi\rangle}$ is complete. Examples: $\mathbb C^n$ with $\langle x|y\rangle=\sum\bar x_iy_i$, and $L^2(\mathbb R)$ with $\langle f|g\rangle=\int dx\,\bar f(x)g(x)$.

Cauchy-Schwarz $|\langle\varphi|\psi\rangle|^2\le\langle\varphi|\varphi\rangle\langle\psi|\psi\rangle$ follows from the axioms (script 4.6) and is the engine of the uncertainty relation. A physical state is a ray: normalised vectors $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle=1$ modulo a phase $e^{i\alpha}$.

Operators. An observable is a linear operator $A:\mathcal H\to\mathcal H$ (e.g. $x\,f(x)=xf(x)$, $p\,f=-i\hbar f'$). The adjoint $A^\dagger$ is defined by $\langle f|Bg\rangle=\langle B^\dagger f|g\rangle$ for all $f,g$ (script 4.23). $A$ is self-adjoint (hermitian) if $A^\dagger=A$. In $\mathbb C^n$ the matrix of $A^\dagger$ is the conjugate transpose, so observables are hermitian matrices: $A_{ij}=\overline{A_{ji}}$.

blocks.label: script 4.20-4.24: reality of expectation values defines "symmetric"; self-adjoint is slightly stronger (same domain of definition)

blocks.html: Dirac notation. A vector is a ket $|a\rangle$, an element of the dual space is a bra $\langle a|$, and the inner product is the bracket $\langle a|b\rangle$ (script 4.29-4.31). The outer product $|\alpha\rangle\langle\beta|$ is an operator with matrix elements $C_{ij}=\langle\varphi_i|\alpha\rangle\langle\beta|\varphi_j\rangle$ (HS16 asks exactly this). Insert a complete set as $\mathbb 1=\sum_n|\varphi_n\rangle\langle\varphi_n|$ whenever you need components.

Eigenvalues of hermitian operators (script 4.27). If $A\psi_n=\lambda_n\psi_n$, then $\lambda_n\langle\psi_m|\psi_n\rangle=\langle\psi_m|A\psi_n\rangle=\langle A\psi_m|\psi_n\rangle=\bar\lambda_m\langle\psi_m|\psi_n\rangle$. For $m=n$: $\lambda_n\in\mathbb R$. For $\lambda_m\ne\lambda_n$: $\langle\psi_m|\psi_n\rangle=0$. Degenerate eigenvectors are orthonormalised with Gram-Schmidt.
Why hermitian? Because the possible measurement results are eigenvalues and a measured number must be real. A non-hermitian $A$ would have complex "outcomes".

$[A,B]$ of two hermitian operators is anti-hermitian: $[A,B]^\dagger=[B,A]=-[A,B]$. The combination $i[A,B]$ is hermitian (HS18 Q2(i), 2 pt), and so is $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$. Never say that $AB$ is hermitian unless $[A,B]=0$.

HS22 B.1(a)-(c): build $\hat x=\mathrm{diag}(0,1,2)$ on a 3-point space, show it is hermitian, show a Fourier matrix is unitary ($S^\dagger S=\mathbb 1$) and use $e^{SAS^{-1}}=Se^AS^{-1}$. The whole problem is Hilbert-space linear algebra in $\mathbb C^3$.

check.q: $A$ and $B$ are hermitian. Which operator is hermitian for sure?

options: $\lambda_{1,2}\in\mathbb R$, but the eigenvectors need not be orthogonal

encounters.title: Spectral decomposition, projectors and the measurement postulate

blocks.html: Let $A=A^\dagger$ on $\mathbb C^N$ with orthonormal eigenvectors $A\psi_n=\lambda_n\psi_n$. The spectral projectors $P_n=|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ satisfy $P_n^\dagger=P_n$, $P_n^2=P_n$, $P_mP_n=0$ ($m\ne n$), $\sum_nP_n=\mathbb 1$ (script 4.32).

blocks.label: spectral decomposition (4.33) and functional calculus (4.42-4.46); e.g. e^{-iHt/hbar}

blocks.html: Measurement postulate (generalised from script 2.7 to 4.35):

Collapse. After the result $\lambda$ the state is the normalised projection $\psi\to P_\lambda\psi/\|P_\lambda\psi\|$ (for a degenerate eigenvalue the projection onto the whole eigenspace, not onto one vector; FS19 Q1(v), 5 pt). An immediate second measurement of $A$ gives $\lambda$ again with probability $1$.

Infinite dimensions (4.6): replace "eigenvalues" by the spectrum $\sigma(A)\subset\mathbb R$, and projectors $P_I(A)$ onto an interval $I$ of the spectrum, $W_\psi(I)=\langle\psi|P_I(A)|\psi\rangle=\|P_I(A)\psi\|^2$. Examples: $\sigma(x)=\sigma(p)=\mathbb R$ for a free particle, $\sigma(H)=\mathbb R_+$ free, $\{E_1,\dots,E_N\}\cup\mathbb R_+$ for a finite well, $\{\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)\}$ for the oscillator.

Compatible observables. If $[A,B]=0$ they have a common eigenbasis (e.g. $\vec L^2$ and $L_z$) and can be measured in any order without disturbing each other. If $[A,B]\ne0$ the order matters (next lesson). A complete set of commuting observables labels the states uniquely.

Probability = squared length of the projection of $\psi$ on the eigenspace. Expectation value = average of the eigenvalues weighted by these probabilities. A superposition keeps both amplitudes until a measurement picks one.

Probabilities add as $|c_n|^2$ for different outcomes, amplitudes add only inside one outcome. The relative phase of $c_1,c_2$ drops out of $W(\lambda_n)$ for $A$, but not for another observable $B$ whose eigenvectors mix them.

check.q: $A$ has eigenvalues $1,3$ with eigenvectors $|a\rangle,|b\rangle$. In $|\psi\rangle=(|a\rangle+2i|b\rangle)/\sqrt5$ the expectation value $\langle A\rangle$ is
The state after measuring $A$ with outcome $\lambda_n$ (non-degenerate) is
options: unchanged, $|\psi\rangle$: a measurement does not disturb
$|\psi_n\rangle$, up to a phase; an immediate repeat gives $\lambda_n$ with certainty

encounters.title: Commutators and the generalised uncertainty relation

blocks.html: Commutator rules (use them to avoid expanding anything): $[A,B]=-[B,A]$, $[A,BC]=[A,B]C+B[A,C]$, $[AB,C]=A[B,C]+[A,C]B$, Jacobi identity. From $[x,p]=i\hbar$ one gets $[x,p^n]=i\hbar np^{n-1}$, $[x,g(p)]=i\hbar g'(p)$, $[p,h(x)]=-i\hbar h'(x)$. If the commutator $[A,B]=c$ is a number, then $[A,e^{B}]=c\,e^{B}$.
Variance. $(\Delta A)^2_\psi=\langle(A-\langle A\rangle)^2\rangle_\psi=\langle A^2\rangle-\langle A\rangle^2$ (script 5.2; HS18 eq. (11)). $\Delta A=0$ exactly when $\psi$ is an eigenvector of $A$.

Proof idea (you must be able to write it): put $\hat A=A-\langle A\rangle$, $\hat B=B-\langle B\rangle$ and $|\psi_A\rangle=\hat A|\psi\rangle$, $|\psi_B\rangle=\hat B|\psi\rangle$. Cauchy-Schwarz: $\|\psi_A\|^2\|\psi_B\|^2\ge|\langle\psi_A|\psi_B\rangle|^2=|\langle\hat A\hat B\rangle|^2$. Split $\hat A\hat B=\frac12[\hat A,\hat B]+\frac12\{\hat A,\hat B\}$: the first part is anti-hermitian (purely imaginary expectation), the second is hermitian (real expectation), so $|\langle\hat A\hat B\rangle|^2=\frac14\langle i[A,B]\rangle^2+\frac14\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle^2$. This is the stronger form (HS18 eq. (15)); dropping the second term gives the textbook inequality.

Position and momentum. $[x,p]=i\hbar$ gives $\Delta x\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$. Equality needs equality in Cauchy-Schwarz ($\hat B\psi\propto\hat A\psi$ with imaginary coefficient) and a vanishing anticommutator term. Solution: Gaussians, $\psi\propto e^{-(x-x_0)^2/4\sigma^2+ip_0x/\hbar}$ with $\Delta x=\sigma$, $\Delta p=\hbar/2\sigma$. For the oscillator state $|n\rangle$: $\Delta x\Delta p=\hbar(n+\frac12)$ (HS18 Q2(iii), 5 pt), minimal only for $n=0$.
$\Delta A\Delta B$ is not about measurement disturbance: it constrains the preparation. No state has both a sharp $x$ and a sharp $p$, because $\hat x$ and $\hat p$ do not share eigenvectors.

The right-hand side depends on the state: for $[A,B]=i\hbar C$ the bound is $\frac\hbar2|\langle C\rangle|$, which vanishes e.g. for $A=L_x,B=L_y$ in a state with $\langle L_z\rangle=0$. Uncertainty relations are state-dependent unless $[A,B]$ is a number.

HS18 Q2 is the template: (i) hermiticity of $i[A,B]$ and $\{A,B\}$ [2], (ii) the relation [4], (iii) oscillator $\Delta x\Delta p=\hbar(n+\frac12)$ [5], (iv) the stronger form [4], (v) check it for $\psi_n$ [3]. See the boss gate.

check.q: In $|n\rangle$ of the oscillator, $\Delta x\Delta p$ equals
options: $\hbar(n+\frac12)$, so the stronger bound $\frac\hbar2$ is saturated only for $n=0$

encounters.title: Time evolution: Schrodinger vs Heisenberg picture, Ehrenfest

blocks.html: Schrodinger picture. States evolve, $i\hbar\partial_t\Psi=H\Psi$, with propagator $\Psi(t)=U(t,s)\Psi(s)$, $i\hbar\partial_tU=HU$. For time-independent $H$: $U=e^{-iH(t-s)/\hbar}$, unitary ($U^\dagger U=\mathbb 1$), and $U$ commutes with $H$. In an eigenstate $H\psi_n=E_n\psi_n$ only a phase $e^{-iE_nt/\hbar}$ appears, so all expectation values of time-independent operators are constant.

Heisenberg picture. $\Psi_H=\Psi_S(0)$ is constant, and the operators carry the time dependence, $A_H(t)=U^\dagger AU$, so that $\langle\Psi_S(t)|A\Psi_S(t)\rangle=\langle\Psi_H|A_H(t)\Psi_H\rangle$. Differentiating and using the equation for $U$ (FS22 Q3(ii), 6 pt):

Consequences. (1) $A$ is conserved if $[H,A]=0$ and $\partial_tA=0$. (2) Commutators are preserved: $[A_H(t),B_H(t)]=U^\dagger[A,B]U$, so a c-number commutator $c$ stays $c$ (HS22 A4, 4 pt). (3) The canonical commutator $[x_H(t),p_H(t)]=i\hbar$ holds at all times.
Ehrenfest in operator form. Taking the expectation value of the Heisenberg equation (or differentiating $\langle\Psi|A|\Psi\rangle$ with the Schrodinger equation, HS21 Q1(ii), 2 pt):

blocks.tex: \frac{d}{dt}\langle A\rangle=\frac i\hbar\langle[H,A]\rangle+\Big\langle\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}\Big\rangle,\quad\frac{d\langle x\rangle}{dt}=\frac{\langle p\rangle}m,\quad\frac{d\langle p\rangle}{dt}=-\langle V'(x)\rangle
blocks.label: for H = p^2/2m + V(x): [H,x] = -i hbar p/m, [H,p] = i hbar V'

blocks.html: Matrix elements between energy eigenstates. Since $\langle\psi_n|[H,A]|\psi_\ell\rangle=(E_n-E_\ell)\langle\psi_n|A|\psi_\ell\rangle$ (FS22 Q3(iv), 2 pt), choosing $A=\vec r$ and using $[H,\vec r]=-i\hbar\vec p/m$ gives $\langle\psi_n|\vec p|\psi_\ell\rangle=\frac{im}\hbar(E_n-E_\ell)\langle\psi_n|\vec r|\psi_\ell\rangle$ (FS22 Q3(v)). For $\ell=n$ the right side is $0$: in a stationary state $\langle\vec p\rangle=0$, the quantum form of the virial/Ehrenfest argument.

The two pictures are two bookkeepings of the same physics: either the state rotates in Hilbert space and the operator stays, or the other way round. Heisenberg is the natural one for conservation laws and for the classical limit, where $\dot A=\{A,H\}$ becomes $\frac i\hbar[H,A]$.

Signs: $\frac{d}{dt}A_H=\frac i\hbar[H,A]$ equals $\frac1{i\hbar}[A,H]$. A common slip is $\frac i\hbar[A,H]$. Check on $A=x$: $[H,x]=-i\hbar p/m$, so $\frac i\hbar\cdot(-i\hbar p/m)=+p/m$ as required.

questions.explain: If $[A,B]=c$ is a number then $[A,e^{B}]=c\,e^{B}$. Take $B=\hat x+\hat p$: $[\hat x,B]=i\hbar$ and $[\hat p,B]=-i\hbar$. Equivalently $f(x,p)=\hbar$-derivatives: $i\hbar\partial_pf=i\hbar f$ and $-i\hbar\partial_xf=-i\hbar f$.

questions.q: Adapted from HS22 A3 (3 pt): $\psi(x)=Ax\,e^{-\alpha x^2}$ is an energy eigenstate of $V=\frac12m\omega^2x^2$. Then
questions.explain: $\psi_1\propto x\,e^{-m\omega x^2/2\hbar}$ (odd, one node), so $\alpha=m\omega/2\hbar$ and $E_1=\frac32\hbar\omega$. Check: $\psi''=(4\alpha^2x^3-6\alpha x)e^{-\alpha x^2}$ and $-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\psi''+\frac12m\omega^2x^2\psi=E\psi$ needs $\alpha=m\omega/2\hbar$ (cubic terms) and $E=3\alpha\hbar^2/m$.

questions.q: Adapted from HS22 A7 (5 pt): $N$ commuting copies $\vec A^{(m)}$ of an angular-momentum algebra, each with $\vec A^{(m)2}=\frac{15}4\hbar^2$. The number of simultaneous eigenstates of all $\vec A^{(m)2}$ and $A_3^{(m)}$ is

encounters.title: Hermitian operators: i[A,B] and {A,B}, real eigenvalues
encounters.goal: Show that $i[A,B]$ and $\{A,B\}=AB+BA$ are hermitian for hermitian $A,B$, and that the eigenvalues of a hermitian operator are real with orthogonal eigenvectors for different eigenvalues.

steps.reveal: $(AB)^\dagger=B^\dagger A^\dagger=BA$. Hence $[A,B]^\dagger=BA-AB=-[A,B]$ (anti-hermitian) and $(i[A,B])^\dagger=-i\cdot(-[A,B])=i[A,B]$.
$\{A,B\}^\dagger=(AB)^\dagger+(BA)^\dagger=BA+AB=\{A,B\}$.

steps.prompt: (c) Eigenvalue equation $A\psi_n=\lambda_n\psi_n$: take $\langle\psi_m|A\psi_n\rangle$ in two ways.
steps.reveal: $\langle\psi_m|A\psi_n\rangle=\lambda_n\langle\psi_m|\psi_n\rangle$ and, by hermiticity, $=\langle A\psi_m|\psi_n\rangle=\bar\lambda_m\langle\psi_m|\psi_n\rangle$ (inner product antilinear in the first argument).

$m=n$: $(\lambda_n-\bar\lambda_n)\|\psi_n\|^2=0\Rightarrow\lambda_n\in\mathbb R$. Then $(\lambda_n-\lambda_m)\langle\psi_m|\psi_n\rangle=0$, so $\langle\psi_m|\psi_n\rangle=0$ for $\lambda_m\neq\lambda_n$.

keyPoints: dagger reverses the order of products and conjugates numbers
commutator of hermitian operators is anti-hermitian, so $i[A,B]$ is hermitian
reality of eigenvalues from $m=n$; orthogonality from $m\neq n$

encounters.title: The Heisenberg uncertainty relation (HS18 Q2 (ii), 4 pt)
encounters.goal: Prove $\Delta A\,\Delta B\ge\frac12|\langle i[A,B]\rangle|$ for hermitian $A,B$ in a normalised state $\psi$.
given: $\hat A=A-\langle A\rangle$, $\hat B=B-\langle B\rangle$ (hermitian), $(\Delta A)^2=\langle\hat A^2\rangle$

steps.prompt: (a) Define the vectors for Cauchy-Schwarz and express the norms.
steps.reveal: $|\psi_A\rangle=\hat A|\psi\rangle$, $|\psi_B\rangle=\hat B|\psi\rangle$. Then $\|\psi_A\|^2=\langle\psi|\hat A^2|\psi\rangle=(\Delta A)^2$ and $\|\psi_B\|^2=(\Delta B)^2$.
$\langle\psi_A|\psi_B\rangle=\langle\psi|\hat A\hat B|\psi\rangle$ (using $\hat A^\dagger=\hat A$).

steps.prompt: (c) Decompose $\hat A\hat B$ into hermitian and anti-hermitian parts.
steps.reveal: $\hat A\hat B=\frac12[\hat A,\hat B]+\frac12\{\hat A,\hat B\}$. Since $[\hat A,\hat B]=[A,B]$, $\langle\hat A\hat B\rangle=-\frac i2\langle i[A,B]\rangle+\frac12\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle$ with both expectation values real.

steps.prompt: (d) Take the modulus squared and drop the non-negative anticommutator term.
steps.reveal: $|\langle\hat A\hat B\rangle|^2=\frac14\langle i[A,B]\rangle^2+\frac14\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle^2\ge\frac14\langle i[A,B]\rangle^2$. With Cauchy-Schwarz: $(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge\frac14\langle i[A,B]\rangle^2$; take the square root.

keyPoints: Cauchy-Schwarz applied to $\hat A\psi$ and $\hat B\psi$
real part = anticommutator, imaginary part = commutator (real/imaginary parts of the same complex number)
$[\hat A,\hat B]=[A,B]$: shifts by numbers do not change commutators
the bound depends on the state unless $[A,B]$ is a number

encounters.title: The stronger uncertainty relation (HS18 Q2 (iv), 4 pt)
encounters.goal: Prove $(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge\frac14\langle i[A,B]\rangle^2+\frac14\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle^2$ and state when it is an equality.

steps.prompt: (a) Real and imaginary part of $z=\langle\hat A\hat B\rangle$.
steps.reveal: $\bar z=\langle\hat B\hat A\rangle$ (hermitian operators). So $\mathrm{Re}\,z=\frac12\langle\hat A\hat B+\hat B\hat A\rangle=\frac12\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle$ and $\mathrm{Im}\,z=\frac1{2i}\langle[A,B]\rangle=-\frac12\langle i[A,B]\rangle$ (the commutator is anti-hermitian, its expectation value purely imaginary).
$|z|^2=\frac14\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle^2+\frac14\langle i[A,B]\rangle^2$ (the sign of the imaginary part drops out).
$(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2=\|\psi_A\|^2\|\psi_B\|^2\ge|z|^2$, which is eq. (15).
Equality in Cauchy-Schwarz iff $\hat B\psi=\mu\hat A\psi$. For $\hat x,\hat p$ and $\mu=-i\kappa$ purely imaginary the anticommutator term vanishes: minimal-uncertainty (Gaussian) states.

keyPoints: real part of $z$ is the anticommutator, imaginary part the commutator
the extra term $\frac14\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle^2$ is the covariance
for $\psi_n$ of the oscillator: $\langle\{\hat x,\hat p\}\rangle=0$, so (15) reads $(n+\frac12)^2\hbar^2\ge\hbar^2/4$

encounters.title: Oscillator: $\Delta x\,\Delta p=\hbar(n+\frac12)$ (HS18 Q2 (iii), 5 pt)
encounters.goal: Show $(\Delta x)_{\psi_n}(\Delta p)_{\psi_n}=\hbar(n+\frac12)$ with the ladder operators and say what is special at $n=0$.

steps.reveal: $a$ and $a^\dagger$ change $n$ by $\pm1$, so $\langle n|a|n\rangle=\langle n|a^\dagger|n\rangle=0$: $\langle x\rangle=\langle p\rangle=0$.
$a^2,(a^\dagger)^2$ change $n$ by $\pm2$ and vanish. $\langle aa^\dagger+a^\dagger a\rangle=(n+1)+n=2n+1$, so $\langle x^2\rangle=\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}(2n+1)$.
$p^2=-\frac{\hbar m\omega}2(a-a^\dagger)^2=\frac{\hbar m\omega}2(aa^\dagger+a^\dagger a-a^2-a^{\dagger2})$, so $\langle p^2\rangle=\frac{m\hbar\omega}2(2n+1)$.

$\Delta x\Delta p=\sqrt{\frac{\hbar}{2m\omega}\frac{m\hbar\omega}{2}}(2n+1)=\frac\hbar2(2n+1)=\hbar(n+\frac12)$. For $n=0$: $\hbar/2$, the minimum of the uncertainty relation (ground state is the Gaussian).

keyPoints: odd/even changes of $n$ kill $\langle x\rangle,\langle p\rangle$ and the $a^2$ terms
$\langle aa^\dagger+a^\dagger a\rangle=2n+1$
only $n=0$ saturates $\Delta x\Delta p\ge\hbar/2$

encounters.title: Heisenberg picture: equation of motion (HS18 Q3 (i)-(iii), FS22 Q3)
encounters.goal: Define $U$, the Heisenberg operator $A_H(t)$, derive $\dot A_H=\frac i\hbar[H,A_H]+(\partial_tA)_H$ and the condition for conservation.
given: $H$ time independent for the formal solution

steps.prompt: (a) Differential equation and formal solution for $U$.
steps.reveal: $i\hbar\partial_tU=HU$, $U(t_0,t_0)=\mathbb 1$. For time-independent $H$: $U=e^{-iH(t-t_0)/\hbar}$ (in general a time-ordered exponential). $U$ is unitary since $H=H^\dagger$.
Choose $\Psi_H=\Psi(t_0)$ constant and $A_H(t)=U^\dagger AU$ so that $\langle\Psi(t)|A\Psi(t)\rangle=\langle\Psi_H|A_H(t)\Psi_H\rangle$ for all states.

$\partial_tU=-\frac i\hbar HU$ and $\partial_tU^\dagger=\frac i\hbar U^\dagger H$. So $\dot A_H=\frac i\hbar U^\dagger HAU-\frac i\hbar U^\dagger AHU+U^\dagger\partial_tAU=\frac i\hbar[H_H,A_H]+(\partial_tA)_H$ with $H_H=U^\dagger HU=H$.
If $\partial_tA=0$ then $\dot A_H=0$ iff $[H,A]=0$: $A$ is a constant of motion. Also, then $\langle A\rangle$ and the whole distribution of outcomes is time independent.

keyPoints: $i\hbar\dot U=HU$ and unitarity
$A_H=U^\dagger AU$ and $\dot A_H=\frac i\hbar[H,A_H]$ (sign check with $A=x$)
conserved iff $[H,A]=0$ and no explicit $t$ dependence

encounters.title: $[x,p]=i\hbar$ is impossible in finite dimensions (HS22 B.1 e)
encounters.goal: Show that no finite matrices $\hat x,\hat p$ satisfy $[\hat x,\hat p]=i\hbar\mathbb 1$.

steps.prompt: (a) Take the trace of the commutator.
steps.reveal: $\mathrm{tr}[\hat x,\hat p]=\mathrm{tr}(\hat x\hat p)-\mathrm{tr}(\hat p\hat x)=0$ by cyclicity.

steps.prompt: (b) Take the trace of the right-hand side.
steps.reveal: $\mathrm{tr}(i\hbar\mathbb 1)=i\hbar N\neq0$.

steps.prompt: (c) Conclude and say what changes in infinite dimensions.
steps.reveal: Contradiction, so $N$ must be infinite. In $L^2$ the operators are unbounded, $xp$ and $px$ have no trace, and cyclicity fails; this is why the uncertainty bound $\frac\hbar2$ cannot be applied for the 3-point model of HS22 B.1 d).

keyPoints: cyclicity of the trace
$\mathrm{tr}\,\mathbb 1=N$
finite-dimensional models have no canonical pair; position and momentum need infinite dimensions

encounters.title: Measurement and spread of $L_z$ in a spin-1 superposition
encounters.problem: An $l=1$ system is prepared in $|\psi\rangle=\cos\theta\,|1,1\rangle+\sin\theta\,|1,0\rangle$ (basis of $L_z$ eigenstates $m=1,0,-1$). Find the outcome probabilities of an $L_z$ measurement, $\langle L_z\rangle$ and $\Delta L_z$. Style: FS26 Q1 (measurement probabilities and uncertainties); the state is chosen here.

derivation.title: Method
derivation.html: $L_z$ is diagonal in the given basis, so $W(m)=\langle\psi|P_m|\psi\rangle=|c_m|^2$. Then $\langle L_z\rangle=\sum_mm\hbar W(m)$ and $(\Delta L_z)^2=\langle L_z^2\rangle-\langle L_z\rangle^2$.

steps.prompt: Which statement gives the probability of measuring $L_z=0$?

why.0: Probabilities are squared moduli of amplitudes.
why.1: That is the probability of $m=1$: the coefficient of $|1,1\rangle$ is $\cos\theta$.
why.3: Equal weights hold only for a uniformly random state, not for this prepared state.

steps.prompt: Order the steps that give $\Delta L_z$.

items.why: Everything follows from the amplitudes in the eigenbasis of the measured observable.

items.text: $\langle L_z\rangle=\sum m\hbar W(m)$ and $\langle L_z^2\rangle=\sum m^2\hbar^2W(m)$

items.why: Needs both moments; a variance cannot be computed from the mean alone.

steps.hint: amplitudes, probabilities, first and second moment, variance.

$\langle L_z^2\rangle=\hbar^2\cos^2\theta$, so $(\Delta L_z)^2=\hbar^2\cos^2\theta(1-\cos^2\theta)$. The spread vanishes for $\theta=0$ (eigenstate) and for $\theta=\pi/2$ (the state is an $m=0$ eigenstate).

encounters.title: Heisenberg picture of the oscillator: $x_H(t)$ and Ehrenfest
encounters.problem: For $H=\frac{p^2}{2m}+\frac12m\omega^2x^2$ derive the Heisenberg equations of motion, solve them and give $\langle x\rangle(t)$ for a state with $\langle x\rangle_0=x_0$, $\langle p\rangle_0=p_0$. Source: HS18 Q3 (ii)-(iii), FS22 Q3 (Heisenberg picture), HS21 Q1 (Ehrenfest).

derivation.title: Method
derivation.html: $\dot A_H=\frac i\hbar[H,A_H]$. With $[H,x]=-i\hbar p/m$ and $[H,p]=i\hbar m\omega^2x$ the equations are linear and closed, so they are solved exactly (as in the classical oscillator).

steps.prompt: Which pair of Heisenberg equations is correct?

why.2: $\frac i\hbar[H,p]=\frac i\hbar(i\hbar m\omega^2x)=-m\omega^2x$: the restoring force.
why.3: The commutator order is reversed; this flips the sign.

items.why: The commutators are the input of the Heisenberg equation.

items.text: Decouple: $\ddot x_H=-\omega^2x_H$ and solve with the initial values $x_H(0)=x$, $p_H(0)=p$
Take the expectation value in the (time-independent) Heisenberg state
items.why: Expectation values come last: the operator solution holds for every state.

steps.hint: commutators, equations of motion, solve, expectation value.
Initial conditions: $x(0)=x_0$, $\dot x(0)=p_0/m$, and the solution of $\ddot x=-\omega^2x$.

why.1: Compute with the solution: the $\sin\cos$ cross terms cancel and $\cos^2+\sin^2=1$.
why.3: A c-number commutator is the same in every state.

encounters.title: The stronger uncertainty relation for spin-1/2 (HS18 Q2 (iv))
encounters.problem: Spin-1/2 in the state $|\psi\rangle=\cos\frac\theta2|\uparrow\rangle+e^{i\varphi}\sin\frac\theta2|\downarrow\rangle$. For $A=\sigma_x$, $B=\sigma_y$ evaluate both sides of $(\Delta A)^2(\Delta B)^2\ge\frac14\langle i[A,B]\rangle^2+\frac14\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle^2$. Use $\langle\sigma_x\rangle=\sin\theta\cos\varphi$, $\langle\sigma_y\rangle=\sin\theta\sin\varphi$, $\langle\sigma_z\rangle=\cos\theta$. Source: inequality (15) of HS18 Q2 applied to spin (the state is chosen here).
symbols: polar and azimuthal angle of the Bloch vector

why.0: The factor $\frac12$ of the relation cancels the 2 of the commutator.
why.1: The commutator is an operator ($\sigma_z$), so the bound is state dependent.
why.2: That is not the commutator expectation value; $\langle\sigma_x\sigma_y\rangle=i\langle\sigma_z\rangle$ and the anticommutator vanishes, but one must use $[\sigma_x,\sigma_y]$.

steps.prompt: Type the anticommutator term $\frac14\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle^2$ (symbols th, ph).

items.why: Independent of the previous steps; gives the commutator term.
The covariance term; needs the means.

items.text: Compare: $\cos^2\theta+\sin^4\theta\cos^2\varphi\sin^2\varphi$ equals the left side exactly

steps.hint: left side, commutator term, anticommutator term, compare.
$\sin^2\theta\cos^2\varphi=\frac12$ for both, so the product is $\frac14$; here the textbook bound $\cos^2\theta=0$ is far from sharp, the stronger bound (0.25) is exact.

encounters.title: Heisenberg uncertainty relation (HS18 Q2, 18 pt)
encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer (2 min per point). Enter the final numbers with $\hbar=1$ for the instances below (the exam asks for general $n$; here you evaluate your general results).
statement: Suppose $A$ and $B$ are two self-adjoint operators acting on a Hilbert space. We define the variance of $A$ via $(\Delta A)_\psi\equiv\sqrt{\langle(A-\langle A\rangle_\psi)^2\rangle_\psi}$, where the expectation value is taken with respect to some state $\psi$ in the Hilbert space.
(i) Prove that $i[A,B]$ and $\{A,B\}\equiv AB+BA$ are hermitian operators. [2 pt]
(ii) Prove the Heisenberg uncertainty relation $(\Delta A)_\psi(\Delta B)_\psi\ge\frac12|\langle i[A,B]\rangle_\psi|$. [4 pt]

(iii) Consider the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator with mass $m$ in the eigenstate $\psi_n$ of energy $E=\hbar\omega(n+\frac12)$. Show that for all $n$: $(\Delta x)_{\psi_n}(\Delta p)_{\psi_n}=(n+\frac12)\hbar$. What is special about the case $n=0$? [5 pt] [Hint: $x=\sqrt{\hbar/2m\omega}\,(a+a^\dagger)$, $p=-\sqrt{\hbar m\omega/2}\,i(a-a^\dagger)$]

(iv) There exists a slightly stronger version, $(\Delta A)^2_\psi(\Delta B)^2_\psi\ge\big(\frac12\langle i[A,B]\rangle_\psi\big)^2+\big(\frac12\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle_\psi\big)^2$ with $\hat A=A-\langle A\rangle_\psi$, $\hat B=B-\langle B\rangle_\psi$. Prove it by considering the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for the vectors $|\psi_A\rangle=\hat A|\psi\rangle$ and $|\psi_B\rangle=\hat B|\psi\rangle$. [Hint: write $|\langle\psi_A|\psi_B\rangle|^2$ in terms of real and imaginary parts.] [4 pt]
(v) Confirm the stronger inequality for the position and momentum operators in the eigenstates $\psi_n$. [3 pt]

finalAnswers.prompt: (iii) $\Delta x\,\Delta p$ for $n=2$, in units of $\hbar$.
(v) Left side $(\Delta x)^2(\Delta p)^2$ for $n=3$, in units of $\hbar^2$.
(v) $\langle\{\hat x,\hat p\}\rangle$ in $\psi_n$ (any $n$), in units of $\hbar$.
(v) Right side of the stronger inequality, in units of $\hbar^2$ (any $n$).

keyPoints: (i) $(i[A,B])^\dagger=-i[B,A]=i[A,B]$, $\{A,B\}^\dagger=BA+AB$
(ii) Cauchy-Schwarz for $\hat A\psi,\hat B\psi$; $\hat A\hat B=\frac12[A,B]+\frac12\{\hat A,\hat B\}$; imaginary part gives the commutator

(iii) $\langle x\rangle=\langle p\rangle=0$, $\langle x^2\rangle=\frac\hbar{2m\omega}(2n+1)$, $\langle p^2\rangle=\frac{m\hbar\omega}2(2n+1)$, product $\hbar(n+\frac12)$; $n=0$ saturates the bound (Gaussian)
(iv) $|z|^2=(\mathrm{Re}\,z)^2+(\mathrm{Im}\,z)^2$ with $\mathrm{Re}\,z=\frac12\langle\{\hat A,\hat B\}\rangle$, $\mathrm{Im}\,z=-\frac12\langle i[A,B]\rangle$
(v) $xp+px\propto i(a^{\dagger2}-a^2)$ changes $n$ by $\pm2$, so $\langle\{\hat x,\hat p\}\rangle=0$ and $\langle x\rangle=\langle p\rangle=0$, so $(n+\frac12)^2\hbar^2\ge\frac{\hbar^2}4$

encounters.title: Heisenberg picture and conservation laws (HS18 Q3, 22 pt)

source.where: Question 3 [Heisenberg picture and conservation laws, 22 pt]

encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer. The final answers ask for one concrete instance of (vi): $l=1$, $s=\frac12$, energy shifts of $\kappa\vec L\cdot\vec S$ in units of $\kappa\hbar^2$.
statement: (i) State the time-dependent Schrodinger equation, and write down the solution with initial state $\Psi(t_0)$ as $\Psi(t)=U(t,t_0)\Psi(t_0)$. Deduce the differential equation the propagator $U(t,t_0)$ has to solve, and construct its (formal) solution. [5 pt]
(ii) Explain how to define the Heisenberg picture, and deduce the equations of motion of an operator in the Heisenberg picture. [3 pt]
(iii) Determine the condition for an observable $A$ that does not depend explicitly on time, to be conserved. [2 pt]

(iv) Consider a Hamiltonian of the form $H_0\equiv H_0(r,\vec L^2,\vec S^2)$, where $r$ is the radial coordinate, while $\vec L$ and $\vec S$ describe the orbital angular momentum and spin operators. Write the components of $\vec L$ in terms of differential operators, and calculate $[\vec L,r]$. Using $[L_x,L_y]=i\hbar L_z$ (and cyclic), show also that $[\vec L,\vec L^2]=0$. Deduce that if $H_0$ describes the Hamiltonian of the system, $\vec L$ is conserved. [5 pt]
(v) Suppose the eigenstates of $H_0$ are $H_0|n,l,m,s,m_s\rangle=E(n,l,m,s,m_s)|n,l,m,s,m_s\rangle$. On which of these quantum numbers do the eigenvalues of $H_0$ actually not depend? Justify. [2 pt]

(vi) Now consider $H_1=H_0+\kappa\,\vec L\cdot\vec S$. What are the eigenvalues of $H_1$ on the space spanned by the states $|n,l,m,s,m_s\rangle$? On which combination of quantum numbers do the eigenvalues of $H_1$ not depend? [5 pt]

finalAnswers.prompt: (vi) Shift of the $j=\frac32$ level of $l=1,s=\frac12$ in units of $\kappa\hbar^2$.
(vi) Shift of the $j=\frac12$ level in units of $\kappa\hbar^2$.
(vi) Dimension of the space for fixed $n,l=1,s=\frac12$ (number of states $|m,m_s\rangle$).
(vi) Sum of all six shifts (with degeneracy), in units of $\kappa\hbar^2$ (check: $\mathrm{tr}\,\vec L\cdot\vec S=0$).

keyPoints: (i) $i\hbar\partial_t\Psi=H\Psi$; $i\hbar\partial_tU=HU$, $U(t_0,t_0)=\mathbb 1$; $U=e^{-iH(t-t_0)/\hbar}$ (time-ordered exponential in general); unitary
(ii) $A_H=U^\dagger AU$, $\Psi_H=\Psi(t_0)$; $\dot A_H=\frac i\hbar[H,A_H]+(\partial_tA)_H$
(iii) $[H,A]=0$ (with $\partial_tA=0$)

(iv) $\vec L=-i\hbar\,\vec r\times\nabla$; $[L_i,r]=0$ because $r$ is a function of $\vec r^2$ and $L_i$ is a derivative along rotations; $[L_i,\vec L^2]=0$ from $[L_x,L_y^2]=[L_x,L_y]L_y+L_y[L_x,L_y]=i\hbar(L_zL_y+L_yL_z)$ and the cyclic partners cancelling; $[H_0,\vec L]=0$
(v) $H_0$ is a function of $r,\vec L^2,\vec S^2$ only: no dependence on $m$ and $m_s$ (rotational invariance, degeneracy $(2l+1)(2s+1)$)

(vi) $\vec L\cdot\vec S=\frac12(\vec J^2-\vec L^2-\vec S^2)$ with $\vec J=\vec L+\vec S$: eigenvalues $\frac{\kappa\hbar^2}2[j(j+1)-l(l+1)-s(s+1)]$ for $j=l\pm\frac12$; independent of $m_j$ (not of $m$ and $m_s$ separately)

encounters.title: QM in finite dimensions (HS22 B.1, 20 pt)

source.where: B.1 - QM in finite dimensions [20 points]

encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer. Enter the final numbers with $\hbar=1$: a matrix element of $T$ and the moments of $\hat p$ in the state $|0\rangle$.
statement: a) [1p] Imagine that the space of positions is discrete, consisting of only three points. The corresponding position eigenstates $|x\rangle\in|0\rangle,|1\rangle,|2\rangle$ satisfy $\hat x|x\rangle=x|x\rangle$. Construct a matrix representation of the position operator $\hat x$ in the $|x\rangle$-basis and show that it is hermitian.
b) [3p] Show that for an invertible matrix $S$, one has $e^{SAS^{-1}}=Se^AS^{-1}$ for any matrix $A$.

c) [7p] Consider the operator $\hat p=S\hat xS^{-1}$ obtained by applying the discrete Fourier transform $S=\frac1{\sqrt3}\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&\omega&\omega^*\\1&\omega^*&\omega\end{pmatrix}$, $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$, to the position operator. Show that $S$ is unitary and determine the matrix representation of $T=\omega^{\hat p}=e^{2\pi i\hat p/3}$ in the basis $|x\rangle\in|0\rangle,|1\rangle,|2\rangle$. What is the action of $T$ on a position eigenstate? Use this to deduce the physical meaning of $\hat p$. [Hint: express everything in terms of $\omega$.]
d) [6p] Calculate the uncertainty of the momentum and position of a particle that is in the state $|0\rangle$. Is the relation of the "uncertainty principle" for positions and momenta satisfied?

e) [3p] Prove that $[\hat x,\hat p]=i\hbar$ cannot hold when $\hat x$ and $\hat p$ are operators on a Hilbert space in finite dimensions. [Hint: recall that for a finite-dimensional Hilbert space the trace is finite.]

finalAnswers.prompt: c) The matrix element $T_{01}=\langle0|T|1\rangle$ (shift operator: $T|1\rangle=|0\rangle$ means 1).

keyPoints: a) $\hat x=\mathrm{diag}(0,1,2)$ real symmetric, hence hermitian
b) $(SAS^{-1})^n=SA^nS^{-1}$ term by term in the exponential series

c) $S^\dagger S=\mathbb 1$ (columns orthonormal: $\sum_k\omega^{(j-l)k}=3\delta_{jl}$); $T=S\,\mathrm{diag}(1,\omega,\omega^*)S^\dagger$ is a cyclic shift, $T|x\rangle=|x-1\bmod3\rangle$: $\hat p$ generates translations (momentum)

d) $\Delta x=0$ ($|0\rangle$ is an eigenstate of $\hat x$); $\langle p\rangle=1$, $\langle p^2\rangle=\frac53$, $\Delta p=\sqrt{2/3}$; product $0$ is not a violation because $[\hat x,\hat p]\ne i\hbar$ in $\mathbb C^3$ (see e)
e) $\mathrm{tr}[\hat x,\hat p]=0$ but $\mathrm{tr}(i\hbar\mathbb 1)=i\hbar N\ne0$
